text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The European Commission could follow Sweden's lead and ban the use of growth hormones in animal fodder with discussions on the issue due this week. The drug Avoparcin is an antibiotic often used in fodder that is banned in Sweden.

- The quality of Swedish exports compared with other industrialised countries has fallen step by step since the 1980s and competitiveness has fallen more than one percent annually, a new study by a business and technical development group, Nutek, has found. Export companies are forced to compete with low prices, but this is not good enough as customers care more about quality than price. The situation is similar in Greece, Norway, Finland and Britain.
- Plans to raise taxes on profits from funds next year from 20 to 30 percent has prompted people to move their savings to different areas.

- The United Nation's torture committee has accused Sweden for the second time in seven months of refusing a victim of torture political asylum. The committee stated on Monday that to not allow the 27-year-old Iranian who fled to Sweden six years ago remain in Sweden would be breaking the torture convention's third article.
- The ruling Social Democrats want to reopen discussions on pensions that were closed about two and a half years ago and make several changes.

- Handelsbanken's chief executive officer Arne Martensson is convinced that the bank's bid on Stadshypotek will go through, he told the paper. He said he was convinced that the bank will have regained its financial strength in two years. Furthermore, the bid will not change the bank's Nordic strategy.

- Two of Sweden's leading banks S-E-Banken and Nordbanken are discussing a merger, which could be implemented already before the end of the year, according to newspaper sources. If a merger is announced, S-E-banken will act as a buyer.
